content:
The stage play "We Are the Happiest," whose performances were cancelled by the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority, was brought to Japan by Mount Seen Bookstore. Yesterday (the 16th), at Home/Work Village in Tokyo's Setagaya Ward, Japanese actors performed the translated script, followed by a creative talk session. Playwright Candace Chong and actor Anthony Wong were present to share their insights, with over a hundred Hong Kong and Japanese audience members in attendance. At the sharing session, Chong was asked about the impact of her work being unable to be performed in Hong Kong. She admitted that her emotions have fluctuated wildly, sometimes feeling very low, but said the experience of being banned has given her a "valuable life experience," which Anthony Wong described as "immersive learning." Chong agreed that the description was apt, adding that "the blows you don't see are even more numerous," to which Wong responded "I feel the same." Chong said she hopes that one day she can write about "all the blows that you don't understand today."

Mount Seen Bookstore has opened a limited-time bookstore called "A Foreign Summer Vacation" (異国の夏休み) at Home/Work Village in Setagaya Ward, with activities including a two-day reading performance of "We Are the Happiest."

Enthusiastic Audience Response, Extra Performance Added

This performance is one of the key events of the limited-time bookstore "A Foreign Summer Vacation (異国の夏休み)" opened in Tokyo from July to September by Mount Seen Bookstore, an independent bookstore that has currently suspended operations. It also marks the latest of Chong's works to be performed in Japan, following earlier productions such as "The First Mirror," and in recent years "May 35" and "Wild Boar."

Mount Seen Bookstore manager Sharon described the catalyst for this performance as a "telepathic connection" with Chong — both hoping to bring good things to Japan to share with others — which led to the reading performance and talk session. Sharon had worried about ticket sales and had not dared to book a venue that was too large, but the first show's over one hundred tickets sold out within two days, prompting a decision to add an extra performance in the gymnasium at Home/Work Village; those tickets also sold out within days.

Mount Seen Bookstore manager Sharon said she shared a "telepathic connection" with Chong, hoping to bring good things to Japan to share, which led to the reading performance and talk session.

Translated Script Read by Japanese Actors; Anthony Wong: "Emotion Has Nothing to Do with Language"

"We Are the Happiest" tells the story of a young gay male couple — trainee barrister Philip and Ah Sang — whose relationship undergoes changes and heads toward a tragic ending after Philip's boss Neil gets involved. The play premiered in 2022, with a re-staging originally scheduled for the end of last year. However, the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority stated that it had received complaints alleging the play "promoted confrontation and smeared Hong Kong," and cancelled the venue and performance.

For this performance, Hong Kong director Indi Chan, based in Japan, condensed the original approximately two-hour production into a one-hour reading, performed in Japanese by three Japanese actors — Shingo Egami (as Neil), Ryosuke Nakanishi (as Philip), and Kikuchi Kanki (as Ah Sang) — who delivered the translated text in script-reading format. After the reading concluded, playwright Chong and Anthony Wong, who was originally slated to play Neil in the play, joined the director and actors for a creative sharing session.

Three Japanese actors performed the translated Japanese text in script-reading format.

Among the ticket-buying audience, roughly one-third were Hong Kongers, with the rest Japanese. While watching the performance, many in the audience opened their Chinese-language or Japanese-language copies of the script to read along with the actors; Anthony Wong was among them. At the sharing session, he recalled a teacher from his time at the Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts who had taught him that "emotion has nothing to do with language." He said this was his first time reading along with a performance in a foreign language, and was amazed that despite not understanding Japanese he was able to follow the pace of the performance, and praised the three Japanese actors' outstanding delivery.

During the performance, many in the audience, including Anthony Wong, opened their Chinese-language or Japanese-language copies of the script to read along with the actors' reading. He was astonished that he could follow the performance despite not understanding Japanese, recalling his teacher's teaching that "emotion has nothing to do with language."

Anthony Wong also expressed hope that "We Are the Happiest" could have a proper production in Japan, joking that he would have to learn Japanese and then play the young role in the play. In addition to the talk session, he also said he welcomed collaboration with figures from the Japanese arts community in areas such as performance. This time he brought eight paintings to participate in "A Foreign Summer Vacation," hoping to hold a solo painting exhibition in Japan next year.

Anthony Wong brought eight Matisse copy paintings on this trip to participate in "A Foreign Summer Vacation," hoping to hold a solo painting exhibition in Japan next year.

Chong: Gained Life Experience from Being Banned; Anthony Wong: "Immersive Learning"

Asked about the impact of her work being unable to be performed in Hong Kong on her creativity, Chong responded that public performances allowed her to examine how her writing was presented, describing it as "the final step in a playwright's learning process during creation." The inability to stage a production has been a major blow to her, who loves the stage. "My emotions have fluctuated wildly; I'm happier here in Japan now, but sometimes I feel very low." As for how she creates under such circumstances, she said she is still "adjusting," but noted that even without being able to perform, she can continue writing, and that she is still creating works.

Drawing on her resonance with the author of "Things in nature merely grow" — whose two sons died by suicide — while sharing her reading of the work, Chong emphasised that the experience of being banned had given her "a different feeling of understanding others' experiences," yielding "valuable life experience." Anthony Wong called this "immersive learning," drawing laughter from the audience. Chong also laughed and said the description was very apt, because "the blows you see are only the blows you see; the blows I myself receive in all areas — the ones you cannot see are even more numerous." Anthony Wong responded, "I feel your misfortune as my own." Chong stated frankly, "All the various blows you don't understand today — one day in the future, I hope I can write them down," adding that she would write them along with Anthony Wong's share as well.

After the reading concluded, playwright Candace Chong and actor Anthony Wong — who was originally slated to play Neil in the play — joined the director and actors for a creative sharing session.

Chong: Feels Setbacks on Gay Situation; Anthony Wong Uses Cha-cha Metaphor

Nakanishi Ryosuke, who performed Philip, said that participating in "We Are the Happiest" reminded him of the Japanese literary classic "The Tale of Genji" from over a thousand years ago, where characters who couldn't attain love would kill others or themselves. He had previously questioned such depictions, but upon finding that a thousand years later, this script from Hong Kong contained the same plot elements, he "started to understand this state of mind a little." Chong explained that although the protagonists are gay, the play's exploration of attachment to love and desire transcends gender and national boundaries.

In response to the change in performance location, Indi modified the original's final act and incorporated background information on laws affecting gay people in Hong Kong and Japan. At the sharing session, Indi mentioned that "whether in Hong Kong or Japan, same-sex couples cannot legally marry," and called on the audience to continue monitoring their rights. Chong stated that in the area of gay rights, she felt that Hong Kong had "in many respects actually moved backwards" compared with other places, and she did not dare to say the next generation would be more open. Anthony Wong used dancing cha-cha as a metaphor, saying "social development doesn't follow a straight line" — moving forward at times and backward at others is the norm.

An audience member wearing a "We Are the Happiest" commemorative T-shirt put questions to Anthony Wong and Chong.

Audience: Good Works Will Always Find Admirers

Japanese audience member Ms. Nakamura Moena had purchased tickets for the originally scheduled West Kowloon performances. After participating in the event, she said she was "very happy to see Japanese actors' interpretation of it in Tokyo," but also recalled "the feeling of not being able to see the performance in Hong Kong at the time." She said she was curious how Anthony Wong would portray the role of Neil, and looked forward to having the chance to see a full stage production in Japan.

Hong Kong audience Ms. So had also purchased tickets for "We Are the Happiest," and extended her stay in Japan specifically to attend the talk session. She considered the performance an example of how many people are still seeking different spaces in which to demonstrate their strength: "As long as it's a good work, there will always be people who appreciate it. Regardless of where it is or in what form, it can move other people."

Japanese audience member Ms. Nakamura Moena had purchased tickets for the originally scheduled West Kowloon performances. She said she was very happy to see Japanese actors' interpretation of it in Tokyo.
